title: Screens, AI, and grade inflation are hollowing out the American high school experience t-american-high-school
author: Amber M. Northern and Michael J. Petrilli
source: The Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 24, 2026
summary: Amber Northern and Michael Petrilli introduce Fordham's report High Tech, Low Standards, a nationally representative survey of about 1,000 current high school students and 1,000 recent graduates, set against Los Angeles Unified's new screen-time limits. The survey yields four findings: illicit tech use is rampant, AI is widely used to bypass rather than support learning, most students spend the majority of class time on school devices, and lenient grading makes distraction and AI misuse worse. Seventy-six percent report daily illicit tech use and 57 percent report mostly A's, including many with low SAT or ACT scores. The authors endorse the report's five recommendations, from reducing device time to relying more on supervised paper and oral exams and enforcing school-wide grading expectations. They add that device-delivered instruction can shrink the teacher into a screen monitor, invoke Theodore Sizer's Horace's Compromise, and argue that the high school experience has become more performative than substantive.
points: Seventy-six percent of respondents report at least one form of daily illicit tech use in high school, and more than one in five use AI without permission.
Over a third use AI to summarize books so they can avoid reading them, and 26 percent use it during quizzes or tests.
Sixty-two percent spend more than half of class time on school-issued devices, well beyond the LAUSD limit.
Fifty-seven percent report mostly A's, including many scoring in the bottom half on the SAT or ACT, so high grades often do not signal mastery.
The authors warn that screens make Sizer's 'Horace's Compromise' easier, letting students check out without leaving the classroom.
quotes: Seventy-six percent of respondents report personally engaging in at least one form of illicit technology use on a daily basis during high school, including scrolling social media, messaging friends, and shopping or gambling online (Figure 1).
Many students are using AI not to support their learning but to bypass it altogether (Figure 2).

Illicit use and sanctioned use are hard to tell apart. When so much of the school day runs through screens, it becomes difficult for teachers to know whether a student is completing an assignment or scrolling TikTok.

Fifty-seven percent of respondents report earning all A’s or mostly A’s, including many whose SAT or ACT scores place them in the bottom half of the national achievement distribution (Figure 4). Put simply, high grades don’t always mean students have mastered the material.

In the hands of a less skilled instructor, technology can shift the teacher’s role from knowledgeable expert who sets high expectations and builds trusting relationships to a classroom monitor who watches students work on screens and tries to enforce on-task behavior.
Today, Horace’s students would have screens to help them sit quietly, making the compromise even easier. In other words, today’s kids can be sitting in class and still be somewhere else entirely.
If classes can be endured by zoning out on screens, assignments evaded through cheating, and high grades awarded without mastery, then we have to ask ourselves: What are we even doing here?!
In other words, we will only solve these problems by restoring the basic conditions for learning: attention, effort, honest work, and adults willing to hold adolescents to high expectations.
